assessment.name: Year 10 Autumn Science Assessment (Chemistry part)
assessment.sections: Thursday 3 December, period 2. Section A: 45 multiple choice questions online across biology, chemistry and physics. Section B: written answers.
assessment.weighting: 60% this term's unit C4.1 Structure and Bonding. 40% Year 9 units: atoms and the periodic table, quantitative chemistry and acids, using resources.
assessment.equipment: Chromebook, black pen, pencil, ruler, calculator

mock.note: 15 chemistry questions weighted 60/40. Do the biology and physics mocks too for the full 45.

group_labels.T: This term: C4.1 Structure and bonding (60%)

leitner_plan.new: C4.1 bonding types, ionic, covalent, metallic (7)

cards.title: Three types of bonding
cards.question: What are ionic, covalent and metallic bonds, and which elements form each?
points: Ionic: metal + non-metal. Electrons are transferred, forming oppositely charged ions.
Covalent: non-metal + non-metal. Pairs of electrons are shared.
Metallic: metals. Positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
cards.watch_out: Look at the elements first. A metal and a non-metal almost always means ionic.
cards.hook: Ionic: I give (transfer). Covalent: co-operate (share). Metallic: a sea of free electrons.
cards.grade9: Explain bond strength by the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged particles.

cards.title: Ionic bonding
cards.question: How do ions form, and how do you draw a dot and cross diagram for sodium chloride?
points: Metal atoms lose electrons to become positive ions. Non-metal atoms gain electrons to become negative ions.
Ions have the electronic structure of a noble gas (a full outer shell).
Group 1 → 1+, Group 2 → 2+, Group 6 → 2−, Group 7 → 1−.
Dot and cross diagrams show one atom's electrons as dots and the other's as crosses, with the ion charge in square brackets.
cards.watch_out: Ions are written with brackets and a charge. Only outer shells need drawing in most questions.
cards.grade9: Use the term electrostatic forces of attraction and say they act in all directions in the lattice.

cards.title: Ionic compounds
cards.question: What is the structure of an ionic compound, and how do you work out its formula?
points: A giant ionic lattice is a regular arrangement of ions held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions.
Balance the charges to find the formula. Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ give MgCl₂. Na⁺ and O²⁻ give Na₂O.
Models (dot and cross, ball and stick, 3D) each have limits, for example ball and stick shows gaps that do not exist.

example.heading: Swap and drop
lines: Al³⁺ and O²⁻: swap the numbers → Al₂O₃

cards.watch_out: There are no molecules in an ionic compound, so the formula is a ratio of ions.
cards.hook: Swap and drop: the charge of one ion becomes the number of the other.
cards.grade9: Compare models by saying what each shows well and what it misrepresents.

cards.title: Covalent bonding
cards.question: What is a covalent bond, and which small molecules should you be able to draw?
points: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms.
Small molecules: H₂, Cl₂, O₂ (double bond), N₂ (triple bond), HCl, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄.
Covalent bonds are strong. Some substances form giant covalent structures; polymers are very large molecules.
Dot and cross diagrams show shared pairs in the overlap of the shells.
cards.watch_out: Covalent bonds are strong. The weak forces are between molecules, not the bonds within them.
cards.hook: Count the bonds: carbon 4, nitrogen 3, oxygen 2, hydrogen 1 (HONC 1234).
cards.grade9: Use molecular formula reasoning, for example ammonia NH₃ has three shared pairs and one lone pair.

cards.title: Metallic bonding
cards.question: How are atoms held together in a metal?
points: Metals have a giant structure of positive ions arranged in a regular pattern.
Outer electrons are delocalised and free to move through the whole structure.
Strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons holds it together.
cards.watch_out: The particles are positive ions, not neutral atoms.
cards.hook: Positive ions swimming in a sea of electrons.
cards.grade9: Link delocalised electrons to three properties at once, conduction of heat, conduction of electricity and high melting point.

cards.title: States of matter and state symbols
cards.question: How does the particle model explain changes of state, and what are the state symbols?
points: Melting and boiling need energy to overcome forces between particles. Stronger forces mean higher melting and boiling points.
State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous solution.
Limits of the simple model: particles are drawn as solid spheres with no forces between them.
At a temperature between melting and boiling point, the substance is a liquid.
cards.watch_out: Aqueous (aq) means dissolved in water, not just liquid.
cards.grade9: When explaining melting, name which forces are overcome (ionic bonds, intermolecular forces or covalent bonds).

cards.title: Properties of ionic compounds
cards.question: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points, and when do they conduct electricity?
points: High melting and boiling points because lots of energy is needed to break the many strong ionic bonds.
They conduct electricity when melted or dissolved, because the ions are free to move and carry charge.
They do not conduct as solids, because the ions are fixed in place.
cards.watch_out: In ionic compounds it is ions that move, not electrons.
cards.hook: Ions must be free to flow.
cards.grade9: State what moves, why it can move and what it carries, in one sentence.

cards.title: Properties of small molecules
cards.question: Why do small molecules have low melting points and not conduct electricity?
points: Small molecules are usually gases or liquids at room temperature.
They have weak intermolecular forces, which need little energy to overcome. The covalent bonds do not break.
Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.
They do not conduct, because molecules have no overall electric charge.
cards.watch_out: Boiling water does not break the O−H bonds. It overcomes the forces between molecules.
cards.grade9: Losing this mark is common. Write intermolecular forces are weak, not covalent bonds are weak.

cards.title: Polymers
cards.question: What are polymers, and why are they solid at room temperature?
points: Polymers have very large molecules. Atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds.
The intermolecular forces between polymer molecules are relatively strong, so they are solids at room temperature.
A polymer is drawn with its repeating unit in brackets and n outside.
cards.watch_out: Polymers are not giant covalent structures. They are very large molecules.
cards.grade9: Compare polymers with small molecules by molecule size and strength of intermolecular forces.

cards.title: Giant covalent structures
cards.question: What are giant covalent structures, and why do they have very high melting points?
points: All the atoms are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds in a lattice.
Examples: diamond and graphite (carbon), silicon dioxide (silica).
Very high melting and boiling points, because many strong covalent bonds must be broken.
cards.watch_out: Melting a giant covalent structure breaks covalent bonds. Melting a simple molecule does not.
cards.grade9: Use the word many. Many strong covalent bonds need lots of energy to break.

cards.title: Diamond and graphite
cards.question: How do the structures of diamond and graphite explain their properties?
points: Diamond: each carbon forms 4 covalent bonds. Very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct (no free electrons).
Graphite: each carbon forms 3 covalent bonds in layers of hexagonal rings, with no covalent bonds between layers.
Layers slide over each other, so graphite is soft and slippery.
Each carbon has one delocalised electron, so graphite conducts heat and electricity like a metal.
cards.watch_out: Graphite conducts because of delocalised electrons, even though it is a non-metal.
cards.hook: Diamond: 4 bonds, rock hard. Graphite: 3 bonds, glides and conducts.
cards.grade9: Compare in pairs, structure then property, for both substances, using whereas.

cards.title: Graphene and fullerenes
cards.question: What are graphene, fullerenes and carbon nanotubes, and what are they used for?
points: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick. Very strong and an excellent conductor, useful in electronics and composites.
Fullerenes are hollow cage molecules of carbon, based on hexagonal rings (also rings of 5 or 7). The first was Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀.
Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with a very high length to diameter ratio. They have high tensile strength and conductivity.
Uses include drug delivery, lubricants, catalysts and reinforcing materials such as tennis rackets.
cards.watch_out: C₆₀ is a molecule, so it has a lower melting point than diamond or graphite.
cards.grade9: Link each use to a property, for example the large surface area of fullerenes makes them good catalysts.

cards.title: Metals, alloys and conductivity
cards.question: Why are pure metals soft, why are alloys harder, and why do metals conduct?
points: Metals have high melting points because of strong metallic bonding.
In pure metals the layers of atoms slide over each other, so they can be bent and shaped.
An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Different sized atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide easily and the alloy is harder.
Metals conduct electricity and heat because delocalised electrons carry charge and energy through the structure.
cards.watch_out: Alloys are mixtures, not compounds.
cards.grade9: Draw or describe the distorted layers. A diagram earns marks in explain questions.

cards.title: Nanoparticles (separate science)
cards.question: How big are nanoparticles, why do they behave differently, and what are their uses and risks?
points: Nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm across (1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m). Fine particles (PM2.5) are 100 to 2500 nm; coarse particles (PM10, dust) are 2.5 to 10 µm.
Nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio. When the side of a cube falls by 10 times, the ratio rises by 10 times.
So smaller quantities are needed and they may have different properties from the same material in bulk.
Uses: medicine and drug delivery, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants, catalysts.
Risks are not fully known. They may be breathed in or absorbed into cells.
cards.watch_out: Learn the size bands with powers of ten, nm and µm. They are often asked.
cards.grade9: Evaluate a use by weighing the benefit (better coverage in sun cream) against possible toxicity and the lack of long-term data.

cards.title: Alloys as useful materials (separate science)
cards.question: What are common alloys made of, and why are they used?
points: Bronze: copper and tin. Brass: copper and zinc.
Gold in jewellery is alloyed with silver, copper and zinc. 24 carat is 100% gold; 18 carat is 75% gold.
Steels are iron alloys. High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon steel is softer and easily shaped; stainless steel (chromium and nickel) resists corrosion.
Aluminium alloys have low density, useful for aircraft.
cards.watch_out: Carat is a measure of gold purity out of 24, not a mass.
cards.hook: Brass zings (zinc), bronze tinkles (tin). Both start with copper.
cards.grade9: Match each alloy to its property and use, for example stainless steel for cutlery because it resists corrosion.

cards.title: Atoms, elements, compounds and mixtures
cards.question: What is the difference between an element, a compound and a mixture, and how can mixtures be separated?
points: An element contains only one type of atom. About 100 elements are in the periodic table.
A compound has two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. It can only be separated by chemical reactions.
A mixture has two or more substances not chemically combined.
Separation: filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation, chromatography.
cards.watch_out: Separating a mixture is a physical process with no new substances made.
cards.grade9: Choose and justify a separation method from the properties given, such as solubility or boiling point.

cards.title: Developing the model of the atom
cards.question: How did the model of the atom change from Dalton to Chadwick?
points: Dalton: atoms are tiny spheres that cannot be divided.
Thomson discovered the electron: plum pudding model, a ball of positive charge with electrons in it.
Rutherford's alpha scattering: most alpha particles passed straight through, a few were deflected. So mass is concentrated in a small positive nucleus.
Bohr: electrons orbit in fixed shells. Chadwick (about 20 years later) proved neutrons exist.
cards.watch_out: Alpha particles bouncing back shows the nucleus is small, dense and positive.
cards.hook: Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr, Chadwick: Don't Trust Rabbits Before Carrots.
cards.grade9: Explain each change as new evidence leading to a new model.

cards.title: Subatomic particles, size and mass
cards.question: What are the charges and masses of protons, neutrons and electrons, and what are isotopes?
points: Proton: charge +1, mass 1. Neutron: charge 0, mass 1. Electron: charge −1, very small mass.
Atomic number = protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons. Atoms have equal protons and electrons, so no overall charge.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
An atom's radius is about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m). The nucleus is about 1/10 000 of that.
cards.watch_out: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
cards.grade9: Use standard form confidently for atom and nucleus sizes.

cards.title: Relative atomic mass and electronic structure
cards.question: How do you calculate relative atomic mass, and how are electrons arranged?
points: Relative atomic mass (Ar) is the average mass of an element's atoms, taking account of the abundance of each isotope.
Electrons fill the lowest shells first: 2, then 8, then 8. Sodium is 2,8,1.
The number of outer electrons equals the group number. The number of shells equals the period number.
cards.watch_out: Ar is a weighted mean, so it is often not a whole number.
cards.hook: Happy Henry Likes Baking Buns, Cakes, Nuts, Oatmeal and Flapjacks: the first 9 elements, H He Li Be B C N O F.
cards.grade9: Show the working with percentages written out. Method marks are given even if the arithmetic slips.

cards.title: The periodic table and its development
cards.question: How is the periodic table arranged, and how did Mendeleev improve it?
points: Elements are arranged by atomic number. Elements with similar properties are in columns called groups.
Early tables were ordered by atomic weight and some elements were in the wrong group.
Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and changed the order where properties did not fit.
When isotopes were discovered, the order he had swapped was explained.
Metals are on the left and form positive ions; non-metals are on the right.
cards.watch_out: Mendeleev's predictions were confirmed when gallium and germanium were found.
cards.grade9: Explain why the table was accepted, predictions that later came true.

cards.title: Groups 0, 1 and 7
cards.question: How do noble gases, alkali metals and halogens behave, and why does reactivity change down each group?
points: Group 0 noble gases: full outer shells, so unreactive. Boiling points increase down the group.
Group 1 alkali metals: react with water to form a hydroxide and hydrogen. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost.
Group 7 halogens: diatomic molecules (Cl₂). Melting and boiling points increase down the group. Reactivity decreases down the group because an electron is gained less easily.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its salt.

example.heading: Displacement
lines: chlorine + potassium bromide → potassium chloride + bromine

cards.watch_out: Group 1 gets more reactive down; Group 7 gets less reactive down.
cards.grade9: Explain reactivity with shells, shielding and attraction to the nucleus.

cards.title: Conservation of mass, equations and Mr
cards.question: How do you balance equations, calculate Mr and explain apparent mass changes?
points: No atoms are lost or made in a reaction, so the mass of products equals the mass of reactants.
Balance equations by changing the big numbers in front, never the small ones in formulae.
Relative formula mass (Mr) is the sum of the Ar values in the formula.
Mass seems to increase if a gas from the air is a reactant, and decrease if a gas product escapes.
cards.watch_out: Burning magnesium gains mass because oxygen from the air joins it.
cards.grade9: In a mass change question, name the gas and say whether it entered or left the system.

cards.title: Concentration and uncertainty
cards.question: How do you calculate concentration in g/dm³, and how do you estimate uncertainty?
points: concentration (g/dm³) = mass of solute (g) ÷ volume (dm³)
1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. Divide cm³ by 1000 to get dm³.
Uncertainty can be estimated as half the range of repeat results, about the mean.
cards.watch_out: Forgetting to convert cm³ to dm³ is the most common error.
cards.grade9: Give the uncertainty with the mean, for example 12.4 ± 0.3 s.

cards.title: Reactions of acids and making salts
cards.question: What do acids react with, and how do you make a pure dry soluble salt?
points: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen
acid + metal oxide or hydroxide → salt + water. acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates, nitric acid makes nitrates.
Soluble salt method: add excess insoluble base or carbonate to warm acid, filter off the excess, heat the filtrate to evaporate some water, leave to crystallise.
cards.watch_out: Adding the base in excess makes sure all the acid has reacted.
cards.grade9: Explain why each step is needed, especially excess and why you do not evaporate to dryness.

cards.title: Potable water and waste water
cards.question: How is drinking water produced, and how is waste water treated?
points: Potable water is safe to drink. It is not pure; it has low levels of dissolved salts and microbes.
In the UK: choose a fresh water source, filter it, then sterilise it with chlorine, ozone or UV light.
Desalination of sea water: distillation or reverse osmosis. Needs a lot of energy, so it is expensive.
Sewage: screening and grit removal, sedimentation into sludge and effluent, anaerobic digestion of sludge, aerobic biological treatment of effluent.
cards.watch_out: Potable is not the same as pure in chemistry.
cards.grade9: Compare the energy and cost of treating fresh water, waste water and sea water.

cards.title: Alternative ways to extract metals (higher)
cards.question: How do phytomining and bioleaching extract copper from low-grade ores?
points: Copper-rich ores are running out, so low-grade ores are used.
Phytomining: plants absorb metal compounds, then are harvested and burned. The ash contains the metal compounds.
Bioleaching: bacteria produce leachate solutions containing metal compounds.
Copper is then obtained by displacement with scrap iron or by electrolysis.
cards.watch_out: Both methods are slow but avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
cards.grade9: Evaluate by giving advantages (less environmental damage) and disadvantages (slow).

cards.title: Life cycle assessment and reducing resource use
cards.question: What is a life cycle assessment, and how can we reduce the use of resources?
points: An LCA assesses environmental impact at each stage: extracting raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, disposal.
Some values are hard to measure, so LCAs can be biased or selective.
Reducing use, reusing and recycling saves resources, energy and landfill.
Metals are recycled by melting and recasting; glass bottles can be crushed and melted.
Sustainable development meets present needs without stopping future generations meeting theirs.
cards.watch_out: An LCA also counts water and energy use and waste at each stage, not just raw materials.
cards.hook: Raw, Make, Use, Bin: the four LCA stages.
cards.grade9: Use data from a table to compare two products, then make a judgement that notes the limits of the LCA.

cards.title: Chemistry calculations to learn
cards.question: Can you write each equation and its units from memory?
points: Mr = sum of Ar values in the formula
concentration (g/dm³) = mass (g) ÷ volume (dm³)
Ar from isotopes = Σ(mass × abundance) ÷ 100
% purity or carat: part ÷ whole × 100
Charges: Group 1 = 1+, Group 2 = 2+, Group 6 = 2−, Group 7 = 1−
cards.watch_out: Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.
cards.grade9: Show every step. Calculation questions give marks for method.

written.q: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point and conducts electricity when dissolved in water.
model: Giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions (1)
Lots of energy is needed to overcome these forces (1)
When dissolved, the ions are free to move (1)
So they can carry charge through the solution (1)

written.q: Compare the structure and properties of diamond and graphite.
model: Both are giant covalent structures of carbon with very high melting points (1)
In diamond each carbon forms 4 covalent bonds; in graphite each forms 3 (1)
Diamond is very hard because of the rigid 3D network (1)
Graphite has layers with no covalent bonds between them, so layers slide and it is soft (1)
Graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon, so it conducts electricity (1)
Diamond has no delocalised electrons, so it does not conduct (1)

written.q: Explain why methane, CH₄, is a gas at room temperature.
model: Methane is made of small molecules (1)
The intermolecular forces between them are weak (1)
Little energy is needed to overcome them, so the boiling point is low (1)

written.q: Explain why an alloy is harder than the pure metal it is made from.
model: Pure metal atoms are the same size and arranged in layers (1)
Layers can slide over each other easily (1)
In an alloy, different sized atoms distort the layers (1)
So the layers cannot slide as easily (1)

written.q: Draw a dot and cross diagram to show the ions formed when magnesium reacts with oxygen, and give the formula.
model: Mg loses 2 electrons to form Mg²⁺ with 2,8 (1)
O gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻ with 2,8 (1)
Formula MgO (1)

written.q: Describe how the alpha scattering experiment changed the model of the atom.
model: Alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil (1)
Most passed straight through, so most of the atom is empty space (1)
A few were deflected or bounced back (1)
So mass and positive charge are concentrated in a small nucleus, replacing the plum pudding model (1)

written.q: Describe how to make pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate from copper oxide and sulfuric acid.
model: Warm the sulfuric acid (1)
Add copper oxide a spatula at a time until it no longer dissolves (excess) (1)
Filter to remove the excess copper oxide (1)
Heat the filtrate to evaporate some of the water (1)
Leave to cool and crystallise (1)
Pat the crystals dry with filter paper (1)

written.q: Compare producing potable water from fresh water and from sea water in the UK.
model: Fresh water is filtered and sterilised (1)
Sea water must also be desalinated by distillation or reverse osmosis (1)
Desalination needs much more energy (1)
So it is more expensive and only used where fresh water is scarce (1)

exam_tips.timing: Section A is 45 questions across all three sciences, so under a minute each. Leave time for Section B.
section_a: Identify the bond type first from the elements in the formula.
For property questions, ask which forces are overcome and how strong they are.
Convert cm³ to dm³ before any concentration calculation.
Cover the options, answer first, then find your answer.
section_b: Explain questions need the structure, then the forces, then the energy, then the property.
For compare questions write a matching point for each substance using whereas.
In method questions write numbered steps with the reason for each key step.
grade9: Never write that covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance melts.
Use precise terms, delocalised electrons, electrostatic forces, intermolecular forces.
Practise unfamiliar substances. Grade 9 questions give data on a new compound and ask you to deduce its structure.

mcq.q: What type of bonding is found in sodium chloride?
mcq.e: A metal and a non-metal form ions.

mcq.q: What type of bonding is found in methane, CH₄?
mcq.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

mcq.q: In ionic bonding, what happens to electrons?
mcq.a: They are transferred from metal to non-metal
mcq.e: The metal loses and the non-metal gains.

mcq.q: What is the charge on a magnesium ion?
mcq.e: Group 2 atoms lose two electrons.

mcq.q: What is the charge on an oxide ion?
mcq.e: Group 6 atoms gain two electrons.

mcq.q: What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
mcq.e: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ balance as 2 and 3.

mcq.q: What holds a giant ionic lattice together?
mcq.a: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
mcq.e: The forces act in all directions.

mcq.q: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
mcq.a: Its ions are free to move
mcq.e: Ions carry the charge.

mcq.q: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
mcq.a: Its ions are fixed in place
mcq.e: Ions cannot move in the solid lattice.

mcq.q: How many covalent bonds does a nitrogen molecule, N₂, have?
mcq.e: Each N needs three more electrons.

mcq.q: Why does water have a low boiling point?
mcq.e: Boiling overcomes forces between molecules.

mcq.q: Why do larger simple molecules have higher boiling points?
mcq.a: Intermolecular forces increase with molecule size
mcq.e: More energy is needed to separate them.

mcq.q: Why don't small molecules conduct electricity?
mcq.e: No charged particles are free to move.

mcq.q: What does the state symbol (aq) mean?
mcq.e: Aqueous means in solution.

mcq.q: A substance melts at −20 °C and boils at 80 °C. What state is it at 25 °C?
mcq.e: 25 °C is between its melting and boiling points.

mcq.q: Why are polymers solid at room temperature?
mcq.a: Their intermolecular forces are relatively strong
mcq.e: Very large molecules attract each other strongly.

mcq.q: Which is a giant covalent structure?
mcq.e: Silica is a giant lattice of covalently bonded atoms.

mcq.q: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in diamond?
mcq.e: This makes diamond very hard.

mcq.q: Why can graphite conduct electricity?
mcq.a: Each carbon has one delocalised electron
w: It has four bonds per atom
mcq.e: Delocalised electrons carry charge.

mcq.q: Why is graphite soft and slippery?
mcq.a: There are no covalent bonds between the layers, so layers slide
mcq.e: Weak forces between layers let them slide.

mcq.q: What is graphene?
mcq.e: It is one atom thick.

mcq.q: What is the formula of Buckminsterfullerene?
mcq.e: It was the first fullerene discovered.

mcq.q: Why are carbon nanotubes used to reinforce materials?
mcq.e: Their length to diameter ratio is very high.

mcq.q: What holds metal atoms together?
mcq.a: Attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
mcq.e: This is metallic bonding.

mcq.q: Why are alloys harder than pure metals?
mcq.a: Different sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide
mcq.e: Distorted layers resist sliding.

mcq.q: Why do metals conduct heat?
mcq.e: Free electrons carry energy through the structure.

mcq.q: What is the size range of nanoparticles?
mcq.e: Nanoparticles are smaller than fine particles.

mcq.q: If the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10, the surface area to volume ratio
mcq.e: Smaller particles have a larger ratio.

mcq.q: Which is a use of nanoparticles?
mcq.e: They give better skin coverage.

mcq.q: What is brass made from?
mcq.e: Bronze is copper and tin.

mcq.q: What percentage of gold is in 18 carat gold?
Why is stainless steel used for cutlery?
mcq.e: It contains chromium and nickel.

mcq.q: What is a compound?
mcq.a: Two or more elements chemically combined
mcq.e: Compounds have fixed proportions.

mcq.q: Which method separates a mixture of liquids with different boiling points?
mcq.e: Liquids condense at different temperatures.

mcq.q: What did the alpha scattering experiment show?
mcq.a: Mass is concentrated in a small positive nucleus
mcq.e: A few alpha particles were deflected.

mcq.q: Who proved that neutrons exist?
mcq.e: About 20 years after the nucleus was proposed.

mcq.q: An atom has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons does it have?
What are isotopes?
mcq.a: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
w: Atoms with different numbers of protons
Different elements with the same mass
mcq.e: Isotopes have the same atomic number.

mcq.q: What is the electronic structure of sodium?
mcq.e: Sodium has 11 electrons.

mcq.q: 75% of chlorine atoms are chlorine-35 and 25% are chlorine-37. What is Ar?
How did Mendeleev deal with undiscovered elements?
w: He ordered by atomic number only
mcq.e: His predictions were later confirmed.

mcq.q: Why are noble gases unreactive?
mcq.e: They do not need to gain or lose electrons.

mcq.q: What are the products when potassium reacts with water?
mcq.e: Alkali metals form hydroxides.

mcq.q: Why does reactivity increase down Group 1?
mcq.a: The outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily
mcq.e: Less attraction to the outer electron.

mcq.q: Which halogen is most reactive?
mcq.e: Reactivity decreases down Group 7.

mcq.q: What is the Mr of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16)?
Magnesium is burned in air and the mass increases. Why?
mcq.a: Oxygen from the air joins the magnesium
mcq.e: Oxygen is a reactant from the air.

mcq.q: What is the concentration when 10 g dissolves in 500 cm³?
Which salt is made from sulfuric acid and copper oxide?
mcq.e: Sulfuric acid makes sulfates.

mcq.q: What gas is made when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
mcq.e: Carbonates fizz with acids.

mcq.q: Why is the insoluble base added in excess when making a salt?
mcq.a: To make sure all the acid reacts
mcq.e: The extra base is filtered off.

mcq.q: What is potable water?
mcq.a: Water that is safe to drink
